source_refs.note: Exercise 11.3, Question 9: book page 295. The book prints no answers for Unit 11.

blocks.prompt: 9 A particle moves along a circular path, described by the position vector \(\mathbf{r}(t) = R\cos\omega t\,\hat{i} + R\sin\omega t\,\hat{j}\). Prove that its velocity is perpendicular to its position vector.
blocks.explanation:
A proof: two non-zero vectors are perpendicular exactly when their dot product is zero.
We need \(\mathbf{v}(t)\) and then \(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{v}\).
Plan: differentiate with the chain rule, compute \(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{v}\), show it is 0 for every \(t\).
steps:
Given: \(\mathbf{r}(t) = R\cos\omega t\,\hat{i} + R\sin\omega t\,\hat{j}\), with \(R\) and \(\omega\) non-zero constants.
To prove: \(\mathbf{v}(t) \perp \mathbf{r}(t)\).
Method: show \(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0\) and that neither vector is zero.

Velocity
\[\mathbf{v}(t) = -R\omega\sin\omega t\,\hat{i}\]
\[\quad + R\omega\cos\omega t\,\hat{j}\]
Why: chain rule, \(\frac{d}{dt}\cos\omega t = -\omega\sin\omega t\) and \(\frac{d}{dt}\sin\omega t = \omega\cos\omega t\).

Dot product
\[\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{v} = (R\cos\omega t)(-R\omega\sin\omega t)\]
\[\quad + (R\sin\omega t)(R\omega\cos\omega t)\]
\[= -R^{2}\omega\sin\omega t\cos\omega t\]
\[\quad + R^{2}\omega\sin\omega t\cos\omega t\]
\[= 0\]
Why: multiply matching components and add; the two terms are equal and opposite.

Neither vector is zero
\[|\mathbf{r}| = \sqrt{R^{2}\cos^{2}\omega t + R^{2}\sin^{2}\omega t}\]
\[= |R|\]
\[|\mathbf{v}| = |R\omega| \ne 0\]
Why: \(\cos^{2} + \sin^{2} = 1\), and \(R \ne 0\), \(\omega \ne 0\). So the zero dot product really means a right angle.

Conclusion and check
Hence \(\mathbf{v}(t) \perp \mathbf{r}(t)\) at every instant: the velocity is along the tangent to the circle, and the tangent of a circle is perpendicular to the radius. A one-line check: \(|\mathbf{r}|^{2} = \mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{r} = R^{2}\) is constant, so differentiating gives \(2\,\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{r}' = 0\).
blocks.final_answer: Hence proved: \(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0\) with \(\mathbf{r} \ne \mathbf{0}\), \(\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}\), so the velocity is perpendicular to the position vector at every instant (it is tangent to the circle).
